title: Field notes: LLM deployments — latency hallucinations & retrieval patterns
content:
Context / why I wrote this:
Quick dumping of observations from recent canary runs (prod-like traffic) + notes from the RetrievalOps workshop (Sept 2027). Trying to capture recurring failure modes and hypotheses to test. Intended for internal teammates (SRE, serving, RAG team).

Top-level observations (high-level):
- We’re seeing correlated spikes in token-level latency and downstream hallucination rate for some routes. Not universal — seems concentrated on RAG/chat endpoints that use chunked document retrieval + long KVs.
- Hypothesis A: KV cache churn + cross-shard retrieval latency introduces synchronized delays that push tokens to slower execution paths (fallback kernels, CPU path), which increases decoding noise and leads to hallucinations in streaming consumers.
- Hypothesis B: Stale or partial retrieval (low-recall first-pass) causes the model to overcompensate with higher entropy generations later in the sequence; timing of retrieval vs generation matters.

Concrete examples from canary logs (summarized):
- 2027-09-07 14:02 UTC, route: /chat/rag-large, p95 token-latency jumped from 70ms -> 240ms for 13 minutes; during window hallucination rate (embedding-match QA) +5% vs baseline. Correlated with a surge in cross-region retrieval calls.
- 2027-09-10 03:10 UTC, route: /embed/similarity, consistent small lat spikes as batch sizes increased from 16->48 due to auto-batcher misconfiguration; not linked to hallucinations but highlighted batching config fragility.

Relevant paper/blog notes (quick skim and takeaways):
1) "On the Interaction of Latency and Generation Quality" (not a formal title — internal shorthand) — concept: quality as function of resource path. Takeaway: fallback to CPU/quantized kernels often coincides with more conservative sampling, but if fallback happens mid-sequence you can get unstable token distribution. Action: ensure kernel transitions are sequence-bound (complete token emission before switching).
2) Retrieval chunking tradeoffs (arXiv/ACL tutorials) — smaller chunks increase recall for exact spans but increase retrieval QPS and latency; larger chunks reduce queries but increase irrelevant context noise. Takeaway: tune per-domain chunk size; add dynamic chunking based on query type (factual vs narrative).
3) "KV Cache Eviction Patterns" (workshop talk notes) — eviction thundering when multiple sessions converge on similar long contexts. Takeaway: probabilistic prefetch + soft-reserve for active sessions mitigates synchronized evictions.

Quick list of links I referenced (copy for later):
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.XXXXX (retrieval chunking survey)
- https://huggingface.co/blog/efficient-kv-caches (blog on KV tricks)
- internal confluence: https://confluence.redwood/example-page-12345

Ideas to test (prioritized):
1) Canary: pin model variant (quantized v2) + force single-kernel path for entire request to avoid mid-sequence kernel switch. Measure hallucination delta. (Owner: serving-runtime)
2) Retrieval: add a two-pass retrieval where first pass selects candidate doc ids (fast, lo-res) and second pass fetches full chunks asynchronously; emit partial tokens only when second-pass ready. Measure latency vs accuracy. (Owner: rag-team)
3) KV cache: implement soft-reserve of top-n sessions during high concurrency windows to avoid eviction storms. Simulate with stressbench. (Owner: sres/serving)
4) Telemetry: add a combined metric that tags token latency with last-retrieval-latency and cache-eviction-count to allow causal slicing. (Owner: observability)

Micro experiments done locally (notes):
- Local simulated shard with 4 clients, artificially delayed retrieval (100ms jitter). Result: models exposed to jitter produced more off-topic tokens after retrieval delays >120ms. Short-term mitigation: buffer streaming outward for 80ms if retrieval in-flight.
- Reduced chunk-size from 512->256 tokens on a docs dataset: marginal recall +3% on exact spans but CPU retrieval QPS up ~1.8x. Might be ok for small customers but not for dedicated fleets.

Conference takeaways (RetrievalOps workshop, Sept 2027):
- People increasingly accept hybrid retrieval architectures (hybrid ANN + exact-recall store) to trade latency vs recall; main pain is consistency under load.
- Speakers recommended adaptive chunking heuristics based on query complexity predictors — there are small models that can predict whether a query is 'span-seeking' vs 'conceptual' with high precision.
- Case study: one team reduced hallucinations by ~6% by dynamically choosing retrieval depth (top-k) and re-ranking by a tiny verification model.

Open questions / probes I want answers for:
- Is the hallucination increase a result of timing jitter alone or is there interaction with the sampling temperature/kernel path? Need controlled experiments where only timing varies.
- How much headroom do we have to introduce small buffering (50-150ms) in streaming without killing UX? Maybe only acceptable for internal tools, not consumer-facing low-latency chat.
- Can we cheaply run a micro verifier that flags high-entropy segments and triggers on-demand retrieval? Cost model needed.

Short-term action items (next 2 weeks):
- [ ] Draft a minimal canary plan for single-kernel pinning and telemetry tagging (me).
- [ ] Add RAG two-pass design doc (rag-team, draft link TBD).
- [ ] Schedule 30m sync with observability to add combined slices (obs).
- [ ] Prototype soft-reserve KV strategy in local bench (SRE + me).

Notes to self (loose):
- When writing the canary, include an opt-in flag so we can toggle kernel-switching behavior per-route. Avoid global changes.
- Track per-token source attribution (which retrieval chunk contributed tokens) — this will make debugging hallucination sources much easier.

End of dump. If anyone (Mika, Eliot, SRE) wants to riff on experiments, ping me. Will turn this into a proper RFC if the canary shows signal.
